title: SEC announces rule to ban players from returning after signing with NFL, NBA, WNBA teams
content:
The SEC has followed the Big Ten — and gone against LSU coach Lane Kiffin — by stipulating that players who signed pro contracts cannot return to a team in the conference.

SEC presidents, chancellors and athletic directors met Tuesday and announced that schools are not permitted to have athletes who:

The SEC said commissioner Greg Sankey was “authorized to enforce this expectation with penalties against member institutions.” It did not stipulate what those penalties were.

The news comes amid various state court injunctions, including in Louisiana, pursued by football players who were in NFL camps and attempting to return to college for what would be their fifth season. Kiffin, set to coach his first game at LSU in less than two weeks, has pursued a couple of those players, including tight end Dae’Quan Wright, who had been with the Cleveland Browns.

Kiffin defended his actions Monday, echoing what players’ lawyers said: that the players did not know the NCAA would change the rule to allow players a fifth year of eligibility. Kiffin also said that if LSU didn’t recruit the players, others would.

But by all indications, LSU was on an island in the SEC. That led to the decision Tuesday, which was preceded by the Big Ten issuing a similar rule.

There was no immediate comment from Kiffin or anyone at LSU, where men’s basketball coach Will Wade has also been pursuing a transfer from former pro RJ Luis Jr., the 2025 Big East player of the year who spent time with the Utah Jazz and Boston Celtics last year.

Notably, the SEC’s statement said it would “enforce” the policy, rather than say it was enacting new policy. The SEC does have a bylaw, separate from NCAA bylaws, that says players who transfer within the SEC must do so during the “regular” transfer window after their season’s end. That would be a way for the conference to argue the Louisiana injunction does not apply to the SEC.

But the conference statement does not lean on the transfer policy – it doesn’t even mention it – and instead focused on the pro aspect. That basically echoed the Big Ten policy, and indicates a confidence it could withstand a legal challenge, if there is one.

This also comes in the backdrop of the SEC discussions since late last year on possibly breaking away from the NCAA, or at least making and enforcing its own rules. This move also shows renewed confidence in being able to do so, if it comes to that. The conference has not given up on the Protect College Sports Act, which would give the NCAA some protection from legal challenges. But self-governance is the SEC (and Big Ten’s) backup plan. This is an early test case for that.

The meeting of SEC leaders in Birmingham, Ala., was previously scheduled, and was due to continue Wednesday.
